analysis.one_liner: Requires data brokers, credit bureaus, and banks to safeguard Americans' personal data and notify them when it is stolen.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. Melissa Bean with 16 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have closed a gap in federal privacy law: companies that collect and sell Americans' Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and driver's license numbers — information brokers — were largely unregulated. It would have brought them under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, required credit bureaus and banks to meet federal security standards, and required written notice to consumers whenever their sensitive personal information was exposed in a data breach, with an exception when the data was encrypted or the company concluded misuse was unlikely.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and card numbers sit in commercial databases. They would learn, in writing and without unreasonable delay, when their information had been compromised, what was taken, and what they could do about it. The bill also would have required companies to verify the identity of anyone buying a consumer report, making it harder for identity thieves to purchase people's personal files.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers at risk of identity theft

how_it_helps.text: It extends Fair Credit Reporting Act coverage to unregulated information brokers that, for a fee, assemble personally identifiable information — including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, and account numbers — and sell reports on consumers to third parties [S2][S3].

It imposes an affirmative, continuing duty on consumer reporting agencies to protect the security and confidentiality of consumers' nonpublic personal information, with the FTC required to write enforceable safeguards within six months of enactment [S2][S3].

It requires credit bureaus, banks, and any business that maintains customer payment account information to send written notice to affected consumers after a data breach, telling them what information was taken, what the company did, and how to protect their files — unless the company reasonably concludes misuse is unlikely, the data was encrypted to federal standards, or law enforcement requests a delay [S3].
It requires anyone requesting a consumer report to have their identity verified under FTC-prescribed procedures, closing off a route identity thieves used to buy personal data [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Information brokers, credit reporting agencies, banks, and any business that holds customer payment data would bear the cost of meeting federal security standards and sending breach notifications. Companies that have been hiding breaches, or selling sensitive data with no oversight, would lose that freedom.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, credit bureaus, and banks

drawbacks.text: The notification requirement contains a large escape hatch: a company that determines after its own investigation that 'misuse of the information is unlikely to occur' does not have to tell consumers at all, and encrypted data is exempt from notification entirely — meaning some breaches would stay secret [S3].

Notice can be delayed at the written request of a law enforcement agency, and notice must wait until the company finishes a reasonable investigation and takes remedial steps, which could push notification weeks past the breach [S3].

Banks, credit bureaus, and data brokers would face real compliance costs for security systems, encryption, and notification programs, and broad over-notification could desensitize consumers to genuine alerts — an objection an honest supporter would have to weigh against the bill's consumer protections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: for the first time, companies that sell Americans' most sensitive identifiers would face a federal duty to protect that data and tell people when it leaks. But the bill was a moderate version of what was circulating in 2005 — the 'misuse unlikely' and encryption carve-outs give companies significant discretion to stay silent, and enforcement rests entirely on FTC rulemaking. It was a meaningful floor, not a strong ceiling.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Melissa Bean introduced the bill on June 30, 2005, joined by 13 original cosponsors including senior Financial Services Committee Democrats Barney Frank and Carolyn Maloney [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, credit bureaus, and financial companies avoided federal security duties and mandatory breach notification for another two years; consumers whose data was exposed in that period had no federal right to be told.

for.name: Rep. Melissa Bean
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 cosponsors for it

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.role: Senior member and ranking Democrat, House Financial Services Committee

against.name: Rep. Michael Oxley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Data broker and financial services trade groups
against.role: Industry lobbies for information brokers, credit bureaus, and banks
against.what_they_did: Opposed strong federal breach-notification and data-security mandates during the 109th Congress, favoring narrower or weaker alternatives

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor — 17 members — was a House Democrat, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call exists; it died in a committee controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: These companies made money assembling and selling Americans' Social Security numbers, account numbers, and license numbers with almost no federal oversight; the bill would have subjected them to the Fair Credit Reporting Act for the first time, ending that unregulated business model.

The bill would impose an affirmative duty to secure nonpublic personal information, require FTC-mandated safeguards, and force them to notify consumers of breaches — compliance costs they avoided under then-current law.

They would have to adopt encryption, monitor accounts after breaches, and send written notices to every affected customer; the encryption safe harbor and 'misuse unlikely' exception softened but did not eliminate the cost.
